title: Conformations and Stereochemistry
description: The three-dimensional shape of molecules: rotamers, rings, chirality and stereoisomers.
overview: Two molecules can have the same atoms joined in the same order and still be different substances. Thalidomide was sold as a sedative, and one of its mirror-image forms relieves morning sickness while the other causes birth defects. Biological receptors, enzymes and our own sense of smell distinguish the two forms: (R)-carvone smells of spearmint and (S)-carvone of caraway.

This chapter covers molecular shape at two levels. Conformational analysis describes the shapes a molecule takes by rotating about single bonds, which interconvert rapidly. Stereochemistry deals with configuration, differences that cannot be undone without breaking bonds: chirality, enantiomers, diastereomers and the stereochemical consequences of reactions.
objectives: Draw and interpret Newman projections and the energy profile of butane.
Explain ring strain and draw the chair conformation of cyclohexane with axial and equatorial positions.
Use A-values to find the preferred conformation of a substituted cyclohexane.
Identify stereocenters and assign R/S and E/Z configurations.
Distinguish enantiomers, diastereomers and meso compounds, and use Fischer projections.
Calculate specific rotation and enantiomeric excess.
Describe the stereochemical outcome of common reaction types.

sections.title: Conformations of acyclic molecules
body: Atoms joined by a single bond can rotate about it. The different arrangements that result are **conformations** (conformers or rotamers). They interconvert so rapidly at room temperature that they cannot be isolated, but their relative energies determine the shape most molecules adopt.

A **Newman projection** looks down one C–C bond: the front carbon is a point where three bonds meet, the rear carbon a circle behind it. The **dihedral angle** is the angle between a substituent on the front carbon and one on the rear. In a **staggered** conformation the bonds are 60° apart, and in an **eclipsed** conformation they line up (0°). Staggered is lower in energy, by about 12 kJ mol⁻¹ in ethane, because of torsional strain: eclipsed C–H bonds repel each other, and in the staggered form C–H bonding orbitals overlap favorably with neighboring C–H antibonding orbitals (hyperconjugation).

In butane, rotation about C2–C3 gives an energy profile with two distinct staggered forms. In the **anti** conformation the two methyl groups are 180° apart, the lowest-energy arrangement. In the **gauche** conformation they are 60° apart and about 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹ higher in energy, because of steric strain between the methyls. The fully eclipsed form (methyls at 0°) is the maximum, 19 kJ mol⁻¹ above anti.

body: At room temperature, about 70% of butane molecules are anti and 30% gauche, since ΔG = 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹ gives a ratio of e^{−3800/RT} = 0.22 per gauche form. Larger groups are more strongly pushed to the anti arrangement, which is why long hydrocarbon chains adopt zigzag shapes in crystals.

sections.title: Rings and ring strain
body: Small rings are strained, meaning less stable than a comparable strain-free chain. Three kinds of strain add up to the **ring strain**:

list: **Angle strain**: the bond angles are forced away from the tetrahedral 109.5°. In cyclopropane, the C–C–C angle is 60°.
**Torsional strain**: bonds on adjacent carbons are eclipsed rather than staggered.
**Steric strain**: atoms or groups are forced too close together.

body: Ring strain is measured from the heat of combustion per CH₂ group, compared with 658.6 kJ mol⁻¹ for the strain-free chain unit:

The strain explains why cyclopropane and cyclobutane open readily (the strain energy drives the reaction), and why strained rings like epoxides are reactive. Cyclohexane is special: it can adopt a conformation with no strain at all.

check.a: Its 60° bond angles and eclipsed bonds give it large ring strain
wrong: It has a C=C double bond

sections.title: Cyclohexane and substituted cyclohexanes
body: Cyclohexane is not flat. In the **chair conformation** all C–C–C angles are about 111° and all neighboring C–H bonds are staggered, so there is no angle or torsional strain. Each carbon bears one **axial** bond, parallel to the ring’s axis and alternating up and down, and one **equatorial** bond, pointing outward roughly in the plane of the ring.

body: A chair undergoes a **ring flip** (chair flip) at room temperature, about 10⁵ times a second. All axial bonds become equatorial and vice versa, through twist-boat and boat intermediates 23–30 kJ mol⁻¹ higher. A **boat** is destabilized by eclipsing and by steric repulsion between the two flagpole hydrogens.

A substituent is more comfortable equatorial. In the axial position it comes within van der Waals contact of the two axial hydrogens on the same face, two **1,3-diaxial interactions**. The energy cost of putting a group axial is its **A-value**:

body: The tert-butyl group is so large that it effectively locks the ring in the conformation with that group equatorial.

example.title: Disubstituted cyclohexanes
example.problem: Draw the more stable chair of cis-1-tert-butyl-4-methylcyclohexane and of trans-1-tert-butyl-4-methylcyclohexane, and estimate how much less stable the cis isomer is.
solution: In the 1,4 relationship, trans means diequatorial or diaxial, and cis means one axial and one equatorial (cis-1,4 and trans-1,3 are axial/equatorial; trans-1,4, cis-1,3 and trans-1,2 can be diequatorial).

The trans isomer sits in the diequatorial chair, with no 1,3-diaxial strain. In the cis isomer the tert-butyl group is equatorial and the methyl is forced axial, costing the A-value of methyl, about 7.3 kJ mol⁻¹. The trans isomer is more stable by this amount.

body: Fused rings: **decalin** (two fused cyclohexanes) occurs as cis and trans isomers. In trans-decalin both rings are locked in chairs, and it cannot ring flip. Steroids have this kind of rigid trans-fused framework.

sections.title: Chirality and enantiomers
body: An object is **chiral** if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like a left and a right hand. A molecule is chiral if its mirror image is a different molecule. The usual cause is a **stereocenter**: a carbon bonded to four different groups. The two mirror-image forms are **enantiomers**. A molecule with a stereocenter and a plane of symmetry elsewhere is **achiral**: 2-propanol has two identical methyl groups on its central carbon and is achiral, while 2-butanol is chiral.

Enantiomers have identical physical properties (melting point, boiling point, solubility, NMR spectrum) in an achiral environment. They differ in two ways: they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions (**optical activity**), and they react differently with other chiral molecules, as in the drug and odor examples above.
A **polarimeter** measures the rotation α of plane-polarized light passing through a sample. The **specific rotation** [α] is the standardized value:

body.eq: [α] = α / (l · c)     (l in dm, c in g mL⁻¹)

body: The sign (+, dextrorotatory, or −, levorotatory) is measured, and cannot be deduced from the R/S label. A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers, a **racemic mixture** (racemate), is optically inactive. The purity of a mixture is expressed as the **enantiomeric excess**:

example.title: Specific rotation and ee
example.problem: A solution of 0.50 g/mL of a pure chiral compound in a 1.0 dm tube rotates light by +6.0°. A different sample has [α] = +9.0° where the pure compound has +12.0°. Find the specific rotation and the composition of the second sample.
solution: A 75% ee means 87.5% of the major enantiomer and 12.5% of the minor (75% excess plus an equal 25% racemic part).

sections.title: R/S and E/Z nomenclature
body: The **Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) rules** assign a unique descriptor to each stereocenter.

list: Rank the four groups on the stereocenter by atomic number of the first atom attached (I > Br > Cl > S > F > O > N > C > H).

Break ties by moving outward: compare the sets of atoms attached to the tied atoms, in order of decreasing atomic number, until a difference appears. A double bond counts as two single bonds, with the atom duplicated at each end.
Orient the molecule with the lowest-priority group pointing away from you. Read 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise is **R** (rectus), counterclockwise is **S** (sinister).

example.title: Ranking by CIP rules
example.solution: All four attach through carbon. The substituent sets on that carbon are {O,H,H} for CH₂OH, {C,C,H} for vinyl (with the duplicate C), {C,C,H} for isopropyl and {H,H,H} for methyl. CH₂OH wins at the first point of difference (O > C), and methyl is last. Vinyl and isopropyl tie, so explore outward: the vinyl CH₂ carries {C(dup),H,H} and the isopropyl CH₃ carries {H,H,H}, so vinyl ranks higher. Order: CH₂OH > CH=CH₂ > CH(CH₃)₂ > CH₃.

body: Natural L-alanine is (S): the priorities are NH₂ > COOH > CH₃ > H. (R)- and (S)- are labels of geometry, not of the sign of rotation. (S)-lactic acid happens to be dextrorotatory (+), but (S)-glyceraldehyde is levorotatory (−): the same label, opposite signs.

The same priorities describe double bonds when cis/trans is ambiguous. If the higher-priority groups on each carbon are on the same side, the alkene is **Z** (zusammen); if opposite, **E** (entgegen). Cis-but-2-ene is (Z)-but-2-ene. For 1-bromo-1-chloropropene, cis/trans cannot be assigned but E/Z can.

A **Fischer projection** draws a stereocenter as a cross: vertical bonds go back, away from the viewer, and horizontal bonds come forward. The carbon chain runs vertically with the most oxidized carbon at the top. Allowed manipulations: rotate 180° in the plane, or swap two pairs of groups. Swapping a single pair, or rotating 90°, inverts the configuration. Fischer projections are the standard for sugars and amino acids.

sections.title: Diastereomers and meso compounds
body: A molecule with n stereocenters can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other are **diastereomers**. Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers have different physical properties, so they can be separated by ordinary crystallization or chromatography. This is the basis of **resolution**: a racemic acid is treated with a pure chiral base to make a pair of diastereomeric salts, which are separated and then converted back to the pure enantiomers.

Tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH, has two stereocenters. The isomers are (2R,3R) and (2S,3S), which are enantiomers (mp 171 °C, [α] ±12°), and (2R,3S), which has a plane of symmetry. The last is a **meso compound**: it has stereocenters but is achiral and optically inactive, because the two halves cancel. It is a diastereomer of the other two (mp 140 °C). So tartaric acid has 3 stereoisomers, not 4.

body: Two diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one stereocenter are **epimers**; glucose and galactose are C4 epimers. In a ring, cis and trans disubstituted cycloalkanes are diastereomers: trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane is chiral (two enantiomers), but cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane is meso.

sections.title: Stereochemical outcomes of reactions
body: Stereochemistry tells us how a reaction proceeds. A reaction is **stereospecific** if different stereoisomers of the starting material give different stereoisomers of the product, by mechanistic necessity (the SN2 reaction inverts configuration, so (R) gives (S)). It is **stereoselective** if one stereoisomer is formed preferentially over other possibilities, though the mechanism would allow both.

head: Reaction
Stereochemical result
rows: Racemization at the carbon (planar carbocation), usually with some excess of inversion
Anti-periplanar H and leaving group; gives a specific alkene geometry
Syn addition of two H atoms to the same face
Syn: the two C–O bonds form on one face
Syn addition of H and OH
table.caption: Stereochemical outcomes.

body: A reaction that makes a new stereocenter from an achiral starting material, using achiral reagents, gives a racemic mixture, because the two faces of a planar sp² center are equally accessible. If the substrate already has a stereocenter, the faces are not equivalent (they are diastereotopic), and one diastereomer predominates (**diastereoselective**). For nucleophilic addition to a chiral aldehyde or ketone, the **Felkin–Anh model** predicts the favored face: the nucleophile attacks anti to the largest group on the adjacent stereocenter, at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle (about 107°) to the C=O. The older Cram’s rule gives the same prediction in simple cases.

Making a single enantiomer from achiral starting materials requires a chiral influence. **Asymmetric (enantioselective) synthesis** uses either a **chiral auxiliary**, a removable chiral group attached to the substrate that directs the stereochemistry (Evans oxazolidinones for aldol and alkylation reactions), or a chiral catalyst, such as a metal with a chiral ligand (Sharpless epoxidation, Noyori hydrogenation, both Nobel Prize chemistry, 2001) or an enzyme. A chiral catalyst is the better solution since a small amount makes a large amount of product. The success is measured as the enantiomeric excess.

summary: Staggered conformations are lower in energy than eclipsed. Butane is lowest as anti, with gauche 3.8 kJ/mol higher.
Ring strain is angle, torsional and steric strain. Cyclohexane in the chair form has none. Substituents prefer equatorial positions by their A-value.
A stereocenter has four different groups. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images with equal and opposite rotation. A racemic mixture is optically inactive.
CIP rules assign R/S and E/Z by atomic number priority. A meso compound has stereocenters but is achiral.
Diastereomers differ in physical properties and can be separated, which is the basis of resolution.
SN2 inverts, SN1 racemizes, hydrogenation is syn and bromination is anti. Asymmetric synthesis needs a chiral auxiliary or catalyst.

problems.q: Assign R or S to (a) CHBrClF drawn with H pointing away and Br → Cl → F running clockwise, (b) (+)-lactic acid with OH → COOH → CH₃ running counterclockwise when H points away.
problems.solution: (a) Priorities Br > Cl > F > H. Clockwise with H away: R. (b) Priorities OH > COOH > CH₃ > H. Counterclockwise: S.

problems.q: trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane and cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane: which is more stable, and by how much?
problems.solution: In a 1,3 relationship, cis is diequatorial (or diaxial) and trans is axial/equatorial. The cis isomer’s diequatorial chair has no 1,3-diaxial strain. The trans isomer has one axial methyl in either chair: about 7.3 kJ mol⁻¹ less stable.
problems.a: cis-1,3 is more stable by about 7.3 kJ/mol.

problems.q: A mixture of enantiomers has an observed specific rotation of −30.0°. The pure (−) enantiomer has [α] = −50.0°. Give the ee and the percentages of each enantiomer.
How many stereoisomers exist for (a) 2,3,4-trihydroxypentanedioic acid (HOOC–CHOH–CHOH–CHOH–COOH), (b) 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane?
problems.solution: (a) Three stereocenters give up to 8, but the molecule has a symmetry that makes some meso: 4 stereoisomers (2 meso, 1 enantiomeric pair). (b) Two different stereocenters, no symmetry: 4.
